candidate.answerReason: The equilateral triangle has height sqrt(3)/2. Each constructed triangle has the same base and one-third its area, so its height is sqrt(3)/6. Its equal side therefore has square 1/4+1/12=1/3.

methods.label: Use the area condition to find the height
methods.explanation:
The three constructed triangles are congruent, so each has one-third the area of the equilateral triangle. Since all their bases have length \(1\), the triangle-area formula turns this area comparison into a height comparison.

First let \(H>0\) be the height of the equilateral triangle. Its altitude bisects its base, so the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
H^2=1^2-\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac34,
\qquad H=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.
\]
Let \(h\) be the height of one constructed isosceles triangle. With the same base length and one-third the area, its height is
\[
h=\frac{H}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{6}.
\]
The altitude of this isosceles triangle also bisects its base. If \(s>0\) is either congruent side, another application of the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
s^2=\left(\frac12\right)^2+
\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{6}\right)^2
=\frac14+\frac1{12}=\frac13.
\]
Taking the positive square root, the required length is \(\boxed{\frac{\sqrt3}{3}}\), choice B.
methods.levelReason: Triangle areas, the altitude property of isosceles triangles, and the Pythagorean theorem suffice.

candidate.annotationRationale: The task connects an area condition to an unknown side length, so triangle area and the Pythagorean theorem are the targets. Isosceles-triangle properties justify both base bisections. Altitude meaning and radical simplification support the written method. The argument does not assume that the constructed triangles tile the equilateral triangle.
